mechanism: Core has exactly one node-removal path: however a peer leaves, CConnman::DisconnectNode leads to PeerManagerImpl::FinalizeNode, which unconditionally runs the tx-download manager's DisconnectedPeer, TxOrphanage::EraseForPeer and the Peer-state reset -- MaybeDiscourageAndDisconnect (refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:5171-5207) reaches it like every other caller. We have three retirement paths and only one of them is complete. disconnect-peer (src/networking/peer.lisp:458-482) closes the connection, releases the outbound-protection slot, clears peer-headers-sync, calls bl.mp:orphan-erase-for-peer, and finally funcalls *peer-disconnect-hook*, which protocol.lisp:664 registers as tx-request-disconnected-peer (:639-660). record-misbehavior (:1678-1719) discourages, closes the connection, sets :disconnected and releases the protection slot -- and stops: no hook, no orphanage sweep, no headers-sync clear. ban-peer (:1721-1733) is the same shape and additionally leaves the peer in state :banned, which replace-disconnected-peers (src/node/peers.lisp:749-753) does not reap because it removes only :disconnected. The registration comment at protocol.lisp:662-663 -- "the tracker must observe every disconnect path" -- is false for two of the three.
consequence: A per-peer leak that accumulates and is remotely triggerable. *tx-peer-announcements* and *tx-peer-in-flight* (src/networking/protocol.lisp:382-386) are EQ hash tables keyed by the peer OBJECT, and the only unconditional remover is the hook. In-flight requests do self-heal after GETDATA_TX_INTERVAL, because retry-timed-out-tx-requests (:831-864) walks *tx-in-flight* and erases an entry whose announcers are all gone -- but that sweep never looks at *tx-announcers*, so a CANDIDATE announcement the peer made and that was never requested is never reclaimed: %tx-request-selectable-p (:667-673) requires (eq (peer-state ...) :ready), so a retired peer's announcement can never become in-flight and can never expire. Such an entry is released only if some other route resolves the transaction, which for an ordinary tx does happen -- and for a hash that will never resolve never does. That is the adversarial case exactly: a peer may announce up to MAX_PEER_TX_ANNOUNCEMENTS (5000) hashes that resolve for nobody, trip one of the seven misbehaviour sites, and leave 5000 permanent announcement records pinning its own peer struct, then reconnect from another address and repeat -- so the per-peer cap stops bounding the total. Alongside that the peer's orphans sit until their own timer instead of being dropped at once, and its headers-sync buffer stays attached. ban-peer has no production caller today (grepped: src/networking/package.lisp:290 exports it, two tests call it), so only the record-misbehavior half is live -- but it is live at seven call sites.
evidence: Container /Users/sen/common-lisp/bl-ga11v-misc-s3d, warm image, probe-e.lisp. Three inbound peers each announced 3 transactions nobody else announced (inbound, so the NONPREF delay keeps them CANDIDATE and out of *tx-in-flight*); *peer-disconnect-hook* was rebound to a recorder that still delegates to tx-request-disconnected-peer; then disconnect-peer / record-misbehavior / ban-peer were applied one per peer. Output: (:ANNOUNCEMENTS-RECORDED (3 3 3)) (:DISCONNECT-HOOK-FIRED-FOR ("10.0.0.1")) (:STATES (:DISCONNECTED :DISCONNECTED :BANNED)) (:ANNOUNCEMENTS-AFTER (0 3 3)) (:ANNOUNCER-TABLE-ENTRIES 6) (:PEER-OBJECTS-STILL-REFERENCED 6) (:AFTER-EXPIRY-SWEEP :ANNOUNCEMENTS (0 3 3) :ANNOUNCER-ENTRIES 6). Only disconnect-peer fired the hook; the peer it retired dropped to 0 announcements (the positive control that the hook does the work), while the misbehaved and banned peers kept 3 each and 6 announcement records still hold their peer structs -- and a full retry-timed-out-tx-requests pass reclaimed none of it. Ours: src/networking/peer.lisp:452-482, :1678-1733; src/networking/protocol.lisp:382-386, :639-664, :831-864; src/node/peers.lisp:749-753. Core: refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:5171-5207 and FinalizeNode.
fix_shape: Collapse the three paths into one the way Core has one. Make record-misbehavior and ban-peer end by calling disconnect-peer instead of open-coding a partial teardown: record-misbehavior keeps its noban and loopback carve-outs and its discourage-peer call, then delegates the retirement; ban-peer keeps the banlist write, then delegates. disconnect-peer already releases the protection slot, clears peer-headers-sync, sweeps the orphanage and runs the hook, so nothing new has to be written -- and the release-outbound-protection calls now duplicated in the two callers come out, since doing it twice would trip the underflow warning at peer.lisp:445-449. ban-peer must then set :banned AFTER delegating, or replace-disconnected-peers has to reap :banned as well as :disconnected, or the peer stays in node-peers forever. Independently, make the leak unreachable rather than merely unlikely: give retry-timed-out-tx-requests a sweep over *tx-announcers* that drops any announcement whose peer is no longer :ready, so no future retirement path can strand one. A regression test asserts, for each of the three paths, that the hook fired, the orphanage entry is gone, peer-headers-sync is NIL and *tx-peer-announcements* has no entry for the peer -- with the announcement count before the call as the positive control.
